utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, can you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, case number IT-01-47-T, the Prosecutor versus Enver Hadzihasanovic and Amir Kubura.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar. I'm going to ask the Prosecution to introduce themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, Counsel. For the Prosecution, Tecla Benjamin, Ekkehard Withopf, and Kimberly Fleming, the case manager.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I'm turning to the Defence. Everybody is here for the Defence, I can see.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours. For the Defence of General Enver Hadzihasanovic, Edina Residovic, counsel; Stephane Bourgon, co-counsel; and Alexis Demirdjian, the legal assistant. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. For the Defence of Mr. Kubura, Rodney Dixon, Fahrudin Ibrisimovic, and Nermin Mulalic, legal assistant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. And the Trial Chamber welcomes everybody, all the technical staff as well, the accused, the Defence, and the Prosecution. We shall continue with the cross-examination of yesterday's witness. So I am going to ask the usher to bring the witness in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, sir. You may sit down. Can you hear the translation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, then. So I'm going to give the floor to the Defence so that they may continue with the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Rajic.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV RAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I hope you've managed to have some rest after a difficult day yesterday. Yesterday we've completed our conversation, my cross-examination, that is, by talking about the decision of the HVO. Before we move on to -- no, I do apologise. I can't see the transcript on my screen. Okay, that's fine. So as I was saying, before I move on to other questions I thought I should put to you, I'm just going to ask you to clarify a certain number of things which have emerged from the yesterday's examination-in-chief by the Prosecution. Yesterday you testified about what you knew about the foreign soldiers or Mujahedin in 1992 and 1993. Actually, I would like you to confirm that my understanding of what you said is correct. On page 7, line 14 all through to 17 of the transcript, you said that those people arrived in Travnik in the summer of 1992 and that in 1993 they came in bigger numbers. In 1993, they were walking around armed, they were of a different race, and they were different from the local population. On page 8 of the transcript, lines 5 through to 8, you said that you knew that they came through various Arab humanitarian organisations. You also said that, on page 8, lines 12 through to 20, that those people could be seen in Travnik and the surrounding Muslim villages. For example, in Guca Gora, which is a point of transit, where they went through -- when they went through Guca Gora, and that you had heard that they had a camp in the village called Jezerce. On page 9, lines 16 through to 21 of the transcript, you said that you had never entered their camp because non-Muslims could not go there, and you also went on to say that they would buy arms and weapons from whoever would sell them. And then on the next page, line 24, you described places where various Arab humanitarian organisations had their premises and where such foreigners could be seen. On page 12 of the transcript, lines 7 through to 14, you described the way they looked, the way they dressed. Apart from that, in answer to my questions, you replied that they bought their weapons on the black market and that around the town of Travnik they could have been seen with the people from the religious life. I have just replied -- or rather, repeated these statements, and I'm just asking you to confirm whether this fully corresponds to your knowledge about these foreigners and their presence in Travnik and the surrounding areas in that particular time. This is all you were able to tell the Court about the presence of these people there; is that so?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV RAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not say everything I knew. This is just a part of what I saw and what I know. Also, I would like to rectify a couple of points you've just made in repeating my statement. I did not say that I knew that they came through the humanitarian organisations. I clarified that statement as follows: I believe that they came. I did not make an explicit statement. I said I thought that they came through these humanitarian organisations for the simple reason that I could see them using the premises and spending time in the offices of -- and around the offices of the humanitarian organisations. It means I do not know whether that's the way in which they came, but I think it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. That's clarified. I just wanted you to clarify some of these points, and you have just done so.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do apologise. Maybe I've forgotten to switch off my mobile phone. I do apologise to the Trial Chamber for this mistake.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Now, I would like us to clarify another answer you gave. On page 13 of the transcript, lines 9 through to 23, you replied to the question put to you by the Prosecution as to whether you knew anything about the presence of Mujahedin in a particular village. In order to clarify your answer, I'm going to ask you a couple of questions. Is it true that that village, Orasac, is a small village where, by June, only Croats used to live?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV RAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is that village, which is situated north of the villages Maljine, Guca Gora, and Mehurici?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV RAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not north of those villages. Rather, more to the south-east of Mehurici, east of Maljine, and north-east of Guca Gora, because those three villages are not really all on one side.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that Croats, the inhabitants of the village of Orasac, left the village or started leaving the village in 1993 and everybody left the village by the conflict -- armed conflict in June 1993? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV RAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that you did not visit that village in the course of 1993?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV RAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Actually, the way I understood your testimony - and could you please either deny it or confirm it - you visited the village for the first time with the joint delegation of the BH army and the HVO in January 1996.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV RAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: That was the first time when you saw Mujahedin in that village; is that so?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV RAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In January 1996, you also saw the four-storey building which had been built in the village, and it is an unusual kind of building for those parts, and you described it on page 13 in the lines 18 through to 22. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV RAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was the first time I saw it close up. But I had noticed its presence before, when it was being built, because it could have been seen from the areas that I normally spent time in.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: So, Mr. Rajic, you did not know exactly when the Mujahedin arrived at that village, but you found them there in 1996, when you visited the village together with a delegation; is that so?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV RAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But due to the nature of my work, I was in touch with different representatives of the International Community, the European Observers, UNPROFOR, at the time, the representatives of the International Red Cross, and others. And on the basis of my conversations with those people as well, apart from other indications and indications obtained by military units as well, I obtained that knowledge that I mentioned yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Another question that I'd like to clarify: On page 14, in lines 2 through to 9, you describe what happened at the 9th of April on Holy Saturday 1993 in Travnik. I believe that you can agree with me if I say that it wasn't the 9th but the 8th of April, 1993.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV RAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It may well be. I may not remember the exact date. But I certainly remember the dates, around -- the events around those dates.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that on that day there was a huge meeting of HVO in Travnik and the most prominent representatives of the Croatian Community Herceg-Bosna, the representatives of HDZ, and Ante Valenta, Dario Kordic, and others from the HVO, Blaskic and others, were present there, and also the representatives of the highest political and military structures of the HVO from all the municipalities from the Croat Community of Herceg-Bosna? Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV RAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of it taking place on that day. And Dario Kordic, Ante Valenta, Kostroman, were not commanders of any sort.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't say they were commanders.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV RAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you did say the top military and political leadership, and commanders, and then you gave a list of them, including Mr. Blaskic, who indeed was a commander.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Okay, Dario Kordic was the vice-president of HDZ and vice-president of the Croat Community of Herceg-Bosna and so on. We're not going to go into all that. But you're saying that it did not happen on the same day.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV RAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say it did not happen on the same day, but I don't know that it happened on that particular day.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: But you do remember that that meeting was held with a great deal of security being organised by the HVO and the Croat Community of Herceg-Bosna; is that so?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV RAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember exactly how it was organised, because I can't remember that it was exactly then. I didn't say what I remember. You said that you remembered a great deal of security. I can't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I'm just suggesting this to you. You don't remember that it was on that day, but you do know that that meeting took place at a certain point in April in Travnik. Are you aware of that meeting taking place?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV RAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a sort of meeting at that time. I wasn't in Travnik, but as to whether it was exactly in April or in May or at some other point in time, I really don't know, because I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that after that meeting -- or, rather, that at that meeting it was concluded that the MUP of Bosnia and Herzegovina was to be declared illegal in that area, Travnik included?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV RAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the first time I hear it, from you now.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In most state institutions in Travnik on that day that you remember, did they put up flags of the Republic of Croatia, which is a neighbouring independent state? Is that so?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV RAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, and I can clarify that, because those were not the flags of the Republic of Croatia. Those were the flags of the Croat people from Bosnia and Herzegovina. On the other hand, what you are saying about the state institutions, I don't know what state institution you mean. But I really don't see what state institution there was where, as you say, the flags of the Republic of Croatia were put up. You obviously don't know the difference between the state flag of the Republic of Croatia and the flag of the Croat people in Bosnia and Herzegovina, or perhaps you don't want to see the difference.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I may not see the difference, but I've asked you and you gave me an answer. Then the three flags were taken down and set alight, because the people who did it felt that it was a provocation.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV RAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, look, at that time whatever was a Croat in Travnik, you're quite right, was felt to be a provocation. We are talking about the extremists from amongst the Muslim population, and they did not say they were not extremists, and so they felt that our very existence in Travnik, the existence of any Croats in Travnik, was felt to be a provocation. Unfortunately, they were the dominant people. They were perhaps not in the majority, but they were the ones who were in power and they felt that the reason and the very fact that we were there, it was a provocation for them.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that after the incident with the flags -- so there was an armed conflict between the HVO and some armed forces and two members of the armed forces were killed and a number of them were injured and a number of the HVO members were injured; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV RAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do know that there was some shooting. I did say yesterday that there was shooting in some parts of town. But there was shooting around the objects -- around the premises where the HVO members were staying. For example, the hotel, the hotel of Travnik, and it is certainly not a state institution.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: So if the official documents were to state that this meeting and this event, the burning of the flags, et cetera, were on the same day, in that case you can say that you were not present in Travnik on that day?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV RAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When you refer to that particular meeting, I don't think I was in Travnik, because I don't really remember. And if I were there, I would have remembered.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I'd just like to clarify certain other issues that you have spoken about. You said that after the beginning of the war in 1992 you still held the position of Secretary of National Defence, but in fact you didn't fully perform those duties; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV RAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. I wasn't able to perform them.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In fact, you said that you only performed the duties insofar as it concerned the HVO, insofar as they concerned the HVO. But you weren't involved in Territorial Defence issues or issues that related to the army. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV RAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not correct. There were attempts. I wasn't involved in the attempts, but the War Presidency, which was headed by a Muslim at the time - now he's probably a Bosniak - and the legally elected president, Izet Tamburic, and some people who were elected and appointed, I was among them, we attempted in Travnik to establish a Territorial Defence. The commander of the Territorial Defence Staff in Travnik was a Muslim. He was an acquaintance, a good friend of mine, Caber Zijad. Later he was the commander of the 312th Travnik Motorised Brigade that was part of the BH army. And that group of people attempted -- I as a secretary ordered in the local textile factory -- we wanted to take off the insignia that -- that they had, the Croatian insignia that the Croatians had on their clothes, and the Muslims had religious insignia. We wanted to get rid of these insignia.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. I think that's a good explanation, clarification. You didn't succeed in this attempt.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV RAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Allow me to finish. It will be clearer for everyone. This was ordered. On a piece of cloth, we had the inscription "Travnik Territorial Defence." There were no insignia on these pieces of cloth, no religious insignia or -- for the Muslims or national insignia for the Croats. However, that attempt was not successful. Neither of the parties accepted it. It was an attempt to establish unity. But it was utopian. After that, in Travnik - and this wasn't the case anywhere else in Bosnia and Herzegovina - there was someone in charge of the French Platoon in charge of the monitor mission in Zenica, he said that Travnik was the light in the tunnel. We even managed to establish a joint staff. We couldn't unify the units but a joint staff, a joint headquarters was formed and Sulejman Ribo was at its head. He was a Muslim. And his deputy commander was the late Colonel Ivica Stojak, who at the time was the commander of a Croatian armed unit in Travnik. Unfortunately, he was killed by the people, the same people with whom he was at the checkpoint on the 20th of October, 1992. I'm talking about the year 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You went into detail. You had an attempt. Stojak was killed. A mixed HVO and army commission was formed. You weren't able to determine the real causes at the time or discover who the perpetrator was.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV RAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The real causes of death were established. It was a term where the person was killed. The perpetrator wasn't identified, but the group that opened fire was identified. We even identified the person who had the rifle.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: This is what you found out later on.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV RAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not later on. I was in that group too, so I know about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. But that attempt of yours in 1992 was not successful. At the end of 1992 and in 1993, in the Secretariat of National Defence you were mainly involved in questions relating to the Croatian Defence Council; isn't that correct? That's what your testimony was yesterday.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV RAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was in 1992. In 1993, I couldn't just appear in my office and work as usual.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: For those reasons, which you have gone into now in detail, you were not able to monitor the position, the situation in the army, the changes, the reorganisation that occurred there, and you weren't able to be familiar with the structure of the BH army; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV RAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Partially. But I did find out certain things. I had contact with people. I received certain information that I could obtain, given that I performed the duties that I performed. As far as the brigade structure, I was aware of it. I know how many brigades there were in Travnik, I know which parts of other brigades there were, and I know which units there were from the Croatian and the Muslim side.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: So you are saying that you were familiar with the brigades in Travnik and you probably knew that at the end of 1992 and at the beginning of 1993 the 3rd Corps was formed and Travnik was in its zone of responsibility. Were you aware of this?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV RAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. But you had far more precise information about the HVO, and you knew that in Travnik an HVO Travnik Brigade was formed; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV RAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You also knew that at the beginning of 1993 in Guca Gora the Frankopan Brigade was formed and it had its headquarters in Guca Gora.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV RAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that was in March 1993. But it wasn't a new brigade with new men; it was the Travnik Brigade that had been divided.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Since you knew that the 3rd Corps had been established, you were probably aware of the fact that the 3rd Corps' zone of responsibility also included this area from Zenica towards Travnik, including places such as Guca Gora, from Ovnak to Maljine, Mehurici and Travnik, and there were certain other places, Bugojno, et cetera. Did you know that this was an area covered by the BH army 3rd Corps?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV RAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Would it be correct to say that HVO brigades, first of all there was the first Travnik one and then there was one divided into Travnik and Frankopan Brigade, they also had their zone of responsibility in this area, between Travnik and Ovnak? In fact, both in Ovnak and in Guca Gora and in Maljine; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV RAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But these were brigades of a territorial nature. They only -- they were only composed of people from the -- they were only composed of people who lived in those areas. They didn't have a manoeuvring nature, they were there to protect the people and property in the areas where they lived.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: So the 306th Brigade and the Frankopan Brigade, for example, acted and had their zone of responsibility in the same area, in fact; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV RAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's correct for 90 per cent of the cases.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: From the 8th of June, in that same area, on the road from Travnik to Zenica via Guca Gora, it was also possible to see HVO members carrying out their tasks. They were wearing their uniforms and carrying their weapons; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV RAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: However, at no time during that period did those HVO units ever form part of the 3rd Corps, nor were they subordinated to the 3rd Corps command; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV RAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they -- it wasn't necessary for them to be subordinated to them. That's true.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: So they weren't.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV RAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In response to a question put to you by the Prosecution, you also spoke about an event on the 8th and 9th of June, and you said that on that occasion, with the help of UNPROFOR, you found and buried seven persons from Guca Gora. Would it be correct to say that among those seven persons who had been killed, five of them were HVO members; whereas, the other two were killed in their houses as a result of shrapnel? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV RAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's correct as far as the ratio is concerned, the ratio of soldiers and civilians. But no one was killed as a result of shell shrapnel. They were killed from firearms.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Those are some matters that I wanted to clarify, and they concern the answers you provided yesterday. After the Presidency decision was taken to proclaim the Territorial Defence was the armed force of Bosnia and Herzegovina on the 8th of April, 1993, Mate Boban, the President of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, issued an order declaring the HVO the only legitimate body and all other formations in the territory of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna were declared to be illegal or enemy formations. Please have a look at this document so that I can ask you my following question.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This document is from the Kordic case, and we have it in both the English and B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Rajic, are you familiar with this document that the Prosecution used as an exhibit in the Kordic case? And it was issued by the HVO president, Mate Boban.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV RAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I've never seen this document before. This is the first time I've seen it.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, although the witness isn't familiar with this document, as it is relevant and concerns the decision on forming the HVO, and the witness was aware of this decision, I would like to tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Withopf.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, the Prosecution objects against tendering this document into evidence via this witness. My learned colleague has not even laid any foundation for tendering this document. If the Trial Chamber allows this document to be tendered into evidence, that would mean each party at any point in time during the proceedings can show a document to a witness, the witness says, "I have no idea what the document is about," and the document could be tendered into evidence. That's, in our view, Mr. President, Your Honours, certainly not the way to proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the Defence respond to the Prosecution's comment.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in accordance with the Rules of the Tribunal, the Trial Chamber can accept any evidence if it deems this evidence to be relevant. I understand the comment made by my learned colleague, Mr. Withopf, because this could be a delicate matter, so I would like to suggest something else. If the Trial Chamber considers that it would not be appropriate to have this accept -- this document accepted into evidence, my other suggestion would be that we have it marked for identification at this point in time and subsequently it could be accepted into evidence in the manner suggested by my learned colleague.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We will deliberate after the break, and we will tell you at that point whether we will have it marked for identification or whether it will be tendered into evidence or whether it won't be accepted as evidence. We'll deliberate during the break. The Trial Chamber notes that the witness said that he was not familiar with this document. This is what the witness said.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you, Mr. President. However, this document, which is one of a series of documents that I want to show the witness, has to do with documents that he was familiar with or documents that he will recognise when they are shown to him. As a result of this order, the main headquarters of the HVO -- of the Supreme Command of the HVO adopted a decision proclaiming all formations that weren't HVO formations illegal. Could the second document be shown to the witness. We have a sufficient number of copies in B/C/S and in English. This is a Prosecution document from the Naletilic/Martinovic case.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Rajic, are you familiar with this order which makes all the orders of the command of the Territorial Defence illegitimate under item 5 and these formations in this territory shall be considered illegal?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV RAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't seen this command, this order either.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Given the witness's answer, Your Honour, I'd like to make the same suggestion: As it is a relevant document, could it be accepted into evidence or could it be marked for identification so that the Defence can subsequently show it to the witness, who will then be able to identify it in a regular way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before giving you the floor, Witness, the Defence now, with regard to this document, it argues about these military documents. You were the Secretary of the National Defence Secretariat, and they have a military role. How is it possible that whilst you were carrying out your duties in the month of May 1992 this sort of document escaped your notice? Do you have an explanation that you can give us? You can see my line of reasoning here. You were in a position which was of a military nature, even though there are civilian aspects involved, and there is a document which deals with the military situation, and these documents have been drafted at that time when you were in this job and yet you say that you were not aware of these documents. And afterwards I'll give the floor to the Prosecution. Can you reply to my question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Look, the structure of the HVO at the municipal level at that time was as follows: There was the municipal HVO as a part of the civilian authorities, and it was within that part of the HVO that there were people elected at the previous elections. What was created was a kind of executive power at the municipal level, and I was a member of that. But as a civilian, on the other hand, the military component of the HVO was the Municipal Supreme Command of the HVO, and that was the beginning of the Travnik HVO Brigade. That was the name it had at the time. When I referred to the Municipal High Command, that's what I have in mind, the military component of the HVO. But I wasn't a member there. As I was saying, I was a kind of liaison between the civilian and the military authorities. On the other hand, the reason why I'm saying I had not seen this and why it had not come all the way to my office was for a very simple reason: Probably it had gone directly to the Municipal High Command of the HVO; that is to say, the military part, but not the civilian part of this structure of the institutions for the Croat community at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. You have given us a specific reply to this specific question. Now, as to the admissibility of this document -- these documents, what does the Prosecution have to say?

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Again, Mr. President, Your Honours, we have the very same situation as in respect to the other document. The document was shown to the witness, the witness said, "I don't know what the document is about." He has, based on the question by you, Mr. President, given a reasonable explanation as to why he is not aware of this document. And the Prosecution reiterates its position that by such a way a document cannot be tendered into evidence. And again, my learned colleague has not even laid any foundation why a document which is dated 8 of May, 1992 could be relevant for the Defence case. My learned colleague - and this is in -- would be in compliance with the Trial Chamber's order - first would have to explain the relevance of this document for the Defence case. Such an explanation hasn't been given. The relevance is more than questionable. And certainly by just showing a document to a witness, the witness says, "No, I don't know the document," in such a manner a document cannot be tendered into evidence. The Prosecution objects tendering this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right, then. As I have said, we shall deliberate about the second document as well. You may continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before my next question, I would simply like to say that the comment made by Mr. Ekkehard is not altogether correct, because yesterday, before I started with my cross-examination, I explained and asked the Trial Chamber to allow me to ask these questions as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Rajic, you've just said that HVO -- that the civilian HVO authorities were set up in Travnik and you were a member of that authority.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to witness to be shown the decision about the temporary structure of power and administration in the Croat Community of Herceg-Bosna, published in the official journal of Herceg-Bosna from the month of September 1992. And this is a copy of the official journal which was shown to the witness yesterday as well. This document was obtained by the Defence from the documents relating to the Martinovic/Naletilic case. And in the course of that trial, it was admitted as proof -- admitted into evidence and it was submitted by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Rajic, since you were a member of the HVO as a temporary institution in the municipality of Travnik, were you aware of this decision when it was reached? And the copy that you have in front of you was published in the official journal in the month of September. Yesterday you referred to the fact that you did receive a copy of that OJ. Can you reply to this question.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV RAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps when the decision was actually reached I may not have known, but if I may, I would just like to clarify something in relation to the earlier paper. I'm a bit surprised and have some doubts about the authenticity of this document because the seal that you see here was never an official seal in Herceg-Bosna. I've only just noticed it. And also, when you look at the paper, you have a seal which we never had as the official seal of Herceg-Bosna. So I have some doubts as to whether this document is authentic or not.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I believe that in the Naletilic case it was up to the Prosecution to ascertain the authenticity of this document, so I wouldn't like to go into that at this stage.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So, Your Honour, you will no doubt reach a decision as to whether this document is admissible or not during the break. But now I'd like to go back to my question I asked with regard to this statutory decision about the temporary organisation of executive authority and administration.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. May I come back to the second document. Considering what the witness has just said, the witness is saying that as far as he is concerned this is a false document due to a whole series of technical reasons, such as the, for example, coat of arms of the HVO, and a seal which is not the right one. So he's arguing against the authenticity of this document. The Defence is saying this is a document which was tendered into evidence in the Naletilic case, but it's not because the document was tendered into evidence in one case and nobody criticised it it is considered as 100 per cent authentic. At this stage we shall take note of the comment made by the witness, who is a legal expert as well, I believe, and he has just said to us that he has some doubts as to the -- this document being genuine. We shall deliberate it -- deliberate in a moment, but we'll take account of this decision. Let us come back to the third document. As you have mentioned, there may be civilian provisions here. So you have the floor, madam.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. We have shown this statutory decision of the Croat Community of Herceg-Bosna by the temporary reorganisation of executive authority and administration in the territory of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. It was published in the OJ of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna in the month of September 1992. Previously the witness had said that he was a member of that civilian authority. My question to the witness is this:

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Since the decision was reached on the 15th of May, 1992 and it was published in September, my question to the witness is whether he was aware of the decision when it was actually made or did he find out about the decision once he received a copy of this official journal?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV RAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I found out about this decision before I got the copy of the official journal, but not exactly on the same day when it was published. A bit later, but prior to its publication in the official journal.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Since the witness has now confirmed that he was aware of the decision, I would like to tender this into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right, then. The Prosecution on the third document. The Defence states that it is an official document which on top of it was published in the official journal. The witness says that he had found out about this decision even before it was actually published in the official journal, and there are undeniable civilian aspects and provisions in this document, since there Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. are references to economic matters, financial matters, justice and others, and all this has civilian connotations. Is the Prosecution against this document being tendered into evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, due to the answers given and as just summarised by you, Mr. President, in respect to this particular document the Prosecution has no objection. However, we wish to emphasise that the witness has commented on the authenticity of the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right, then. We shall reach a decision in a moment on the third document as well. You may continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is it true, Mr. Rajic, that in line with this document the executive authority of HVO in May 1992 was set up and thereby HVO was set up as the highest authority, as the highest executive power in Travnik itself? What you have said earlier on, was it all based on this decision of the Croat Community of Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV RAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But I really don't know if it happened straight away in the month of May, but yes, fairly soon. As I said, we set up some of the departments, sort of.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: From then on, there were parallel institutions in Travnik for both the civilian and military authorities; is that so?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV RAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it is not. This parallelism had existed before, not only as of that day.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: These documents that we saw yesterday and the documents that you were shown today, especially the one referring to the executive power, were not approved by any of the bodies elected at the pre-war elections, nor in line with the Constitution and the legal provisions was there any approval from the authorities at the republic level; is that so?

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President. Mr. President, the witness has said in respect to two out of the three documents that he wasn't aware of the documents. The Defence shouldn't be allowed to ask follow-up questions in relation to the two documents. In addition, I wish to draw the attention of the Trial Chamber that the Prosecution examined in chief this witness for one hour and one minute. Meanwhile, Defence is cross-examining this witness for more than 2 hours and 45 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. About the second point, the Defence will have noticed that, in terms of time, you've already spent double the time that the Prosecution had. Obviously the Prosecution will be allowed to make up for that when we have supplementary questions, but we do have this problem of time. As to the first point on documents, considering the situation - I'm referring to the transcript here - following your question, the witness has replied that there was a parallel system which was in existence before this document was drafted. If my understanding of what you are saying is correct, quite apart from the legal authority which was recognised by everyone, within the Croat community there was this setting up of a parallel system but that parallel system, as you have just told us, had already been in existence from before. Could you specify that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I meant to say was that there was this parallelism when it came to the setting up of different military formations. Prior to that moment in Travnik, we had already had the political parties for the two peoples, for the Muslims and the Croats, the leading political parties, and then the SDA, the HDZ, and they were involved in creating this parallelism that I was referring to. And all power, quite apart from us who were members of the executive power, everything was in the hands of those parties. As to the executive, unless we had support and approval from those structures, we were unable to do anything whatsoever. Why were we not in a position to unify the joint command? We even had the joint commanders and the chief of staff and everything, but we did not get support from the political parties. Why were we not successful with the Territorial Defence in the way in which we thought we could do it in Travnik? Precisely because of a lack of such support. And by then we had a certain number of military formations, HOS, for example. And this was nothing that was registered or recorded anywhere in an official way but there was the MOS, the Muslim Armed Forces, as well. So we had the Croat and the Muslim Armed Forces, and they called themselves like that but I am not aware of any official document relating to that. And then we had the Patriotic League, which only had members of the Muslim population. So when I talk about parallelism, this is what I have in mind. And for those of us who were elected in a legal way and legally appointed, we really had no real power. We could not administer or govern Travnik. There were a number of attempts, and we could make those attempts for as long as we had the then-president of the War Presidency, Mr. Izet Tamburic, who was the president of the municipal assembly. And when there was imminent danger of war, he was the president of the War Presidency. And the members of the War Presidency were the commander of the Territorial Defence Corps, who was a Muslim, Caber Zijad, who was mentioned before; and then the Secretary for the National Defence, it was -- I mean, myself; and then the commander of the JNA barracks in Travnik, and I think his name was Jovanovic. He was a Serb, Lieutenant Jovanovic. And then there was a police chief and then somebody from the Department of Trade and Finance. So we had a fairly balanced national structure represented there, in line with the results of the census and in line with the results of the elections after 1990. However, the Serbs very rapidly left that War Presidency because the barracks commander left with the JNA. And until Tamburic was replaced, there was some attempts. But after he was replaced, I don't know who was able to take his place, but someone else became the head of the War Presidency, also a Muslim, and it was no longer possible to work together. And why was it no longer possible to work together? Why was this still impossible? I mentioned that briefly yesterday. The Muslims in Travnik - some of them, not all of them - these Muslims started organising themselves on a religious basis. In the meantime, people from outside started arriving. They wore religious symbols on their clothes. As someone of a different faith, as a member of a different people, I can't be asked to be a member of such a military formation, of such an army. So this is the parallel structure I'm referring to and this is what made us Croats to keep to ourselves and to try and protect ourselves.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I think that your long answer will not make it necessary to ask you certain other questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I think I have another 20 questions out of the 120 questions I had. I think I'll conclude very rapidly. And with regard to the Prosecution's comments, it's true that I have been cross-examining this witness for a long period of time, given his relevance, but there are only a few witnesses that I have cross-examined for more than half the time than the Prosecution. I think the Trial Chamber can understand my position with regard to this witness. Thank you for your understanding. Your Honour, you said that you would take a decision with regard to the statutory decision during the break.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You said that you formed these organs of power. I'd like to show you a decision on the appointment of a president and vice-president of the municipal HVO in Travnik. This decision is one that was included among the Prosecution's documents. It's from the Naletilic case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Withopf.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, can I make a suggestion at this point in time?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm listening to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: The Defence is continuing to show the witness documents and the witness has already said to a number of documents he can't say anything in relation to them. The Chamber has announced that they would deliberate on this issue later on, during the break. It may save court time if the Chamber would deliberate on this issue right now, since this, depending on the outcome of the deliberation, would probably lead to a situation the Defence wouldn't use any further documents. This is just a suggestion, but I think it's necessary, taking into account the time that has passed in cross-examination of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Before I ask the Defence whether there are any other documents, everything said by the witness and all the questions put by the Prosecution and the Defence are of interest. That is quite obvious. With regard to the documents, these documents relate to the period that is relevant to the indictment. It has to do with the duties performed, important duties. As it has been said, there are documents which have been contested. We have taken note of the fact. And with regard to the Prosecution's suggestion, that is to say that the Trial Chamber should deliberate, well, before I answer that question, how many more documents do you have?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Three documents, Your Honours, in addition to the one that the witness has before him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have another three documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I assume these documents are similar to the previous ones, or do those documents relate to other matters?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, these are documents that solve the issue of the documents that we have already seen. One concerns the appointment of Mr. Rajic. So two of the documents are from the territory of Travnik municipality, and two are republican documents. So in total, there are four. The witness has one; and I have others that are from the Travnik municipality, and there are two documents that are related to documents that have already been shown. I can perhaps show all three documents to the witness at the same time and he can tell us what he knows about them and then you can rule on the matter. But perhaps it would be good if my colleague, Mr. Bourgon, addressed the Trial Chamber with regard to the subject of accepting documents into evidence, with your permission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. And with regard to the relevance, because the debate concerns the relevance of the documents, in your opinion, are the four documents relevant?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honours. I'll immediately inform you of the documents concerned. But I'd like to show them to the witness too. One of them is a document that states that under the pressure in August the law on the armed forces in Bosnia-Herzegovina was amended and the HVO was accepted as part of the Armed Forces of Bosnia and Herzegovina, providing the Main Staff of the BH army is accepted as its command. The other documents concerns all the documents that you accepted yesterday and the documents that we saw today from the Official Gazette. It's the decision of the constitutional court of Bosnia and Herzegovina which declared that all these documents were anti-constitutional. And the last one has to do with the appointment of Mr. Rajic to a certain position in the HVO. These are the three documents. I think that the contents I have mentioned show that they are very relevant, that they concern what happened then and later in the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina and in Central Bosnia and concern the relations between the army and the HVO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We have taken note of what you have said. The best thing to do would be to have a break immediately, and after the break we will have deliberated about the documents. But we have taken note of the Defence's objectives, the Defence's purposes with regard to the other documents. Mr. Withopf, is there something you wanted to say before we started deliberating? Because we were just about to leave. Were you getting up because we were going to leave?

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: I'm rising because you are about to leave, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you. Does the Defence want to add anything? Mr. Bourgon? Sit down for a minute. Mr. Bourgon, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Before the Trial Chamber deliberates on the documents that the Defence wants to tender into evidence, with regard to what has happened over the last few days and in the case of several witnesses, we have a few issues to raise with regard to accepting documents into evidence or with regard to marking documents for identification, or we have a few matters to raise with regard to documents that haven't been accepted. So before the Chamber deliberates on the four or five documents that concern this witness, the Defence suggests that the question of documents merits a detailed debate, because this is a matter that we will have before us all the time. The decision you will take in a minute could have an influence or could have repercussions for other witnesses. I suggest that it would be good if we could make a few submissions, both -- if both sides could make some submissions with regard to this matter and with regard to the procedure that should be followed when tendering a document into evidence. It would be good if the Trial Chamber could then inform us as to what they consider to be the correct procedure, and that would enable us to act appropriately. The Defence is quite ready to adapt itself to the decisions of the Trial Chamber, whatever they are. Can the document be accepted on the basis of its relevance, as in other cases, or must a document be identified by the document -- by the witness? Is this absolutely necessary? And it's necessary for the witness to corroborate an element in a document or its authenticity? Whatever the case, this is the procedure suggested by the Prosecution. The Defence will respect the Trial Chamber's decisions, and it won't object to using this procedure for tendering documents into evidence. If the Trial Chamber takes another decision, what would be important for us is that the decision taken by the Trial Chamber is one that will be adhered to until the end of the proceedings. So whatever the case, the Defence will respect the Trial Chamber's decision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before we take a decision on this very important matter, the Chamber would like to know what the Prosecution's position is. As you know, a List of Documents was established before the proceedings started and in the course of the pre-trial proceedings we noted that there were tens or hundreds of documents, in fact. The Defence will certainly be producing other documents, this is quite obvious. We might be in a situation in which we'll have thousands of documents. There are two solutions, as has been pointed out: Either the document -- either documents will be produced as witnesses are heard, and if the witness doesn't recognise or identify a document, the document will be rejected; or the Trial Chamber might deem that the document is relevant, even if it hasn't been identified by the witness, and as a result the document can be admitted into evidence. So there are two different ways of proceeding. We want to save time in the course of the proceedings, and we don't want to have to debate on the matter each time this issue arises. If a document is produced, the Prosecution objects, and then we waste time although the document might be considered to be relevant. Perhaps not at the time it is shown, but it might be considered to be relevant later on, because there will be other witnesses, other expert witnesses, et cetera. So we have an important problem there. We'll deliberate on it immediately. And if necessary, we'll also deliberate on the three documents and provide you with our decision. At the moment, I would like to know what the Prosecution's position is. The Prosecution has already expressed its position with regard to the three documents. It's not necessary to go back to that matter, but as far as the essence of this problem is concerned, it's the Prosecution that has the burden of proof and the Prosecution has to present documents. So naturally, when an expert witness comes - and he'll have had hundreds of documents - then the Prosecution will raise the issue of tendering documents into evidence and will raise the question of the documents referred to by the expert witness. So could the Prosecution clarify the matter. And I'd like to point out that everyone wants to avoid wasting time. So, Mr. Withopf, what do you have to say with regard to this crucial issue of documents?

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, as you were saying, there are different solutions to this problem. And it's actually a legal problem. The first solution could be that both parties tender documents into evidence from the bar table, meaning all the hundreds of documents go in without any witness. That is a pretty practical solution. It's, however, also a radical solution. The second solution could be - and this is what has been followed in the past - that documents are tendered via a witness. In the event the document is tendered via a witness, the witness must be in a position to comment on the document. Only in such a situation, in the Prosecution's submission, a document can be tendered into evidence. The crucial issue, however, is the relevance of the document. Only relevant documents can be tendered into evidence, and it's up to the party which wishes to tender the document into evidence to establish, prior to tendering the document into evidence, to establish the relevance and the likely probative value of such documents. In respect to the documents that have been shown today to the witness, the Prosecution noticed that they stem from time periods 1992, quite a number of them from a time within the first half of 1992. According to my learned colleague, the documents are supposed to show the relations and parallel structures between the HVO and the ABiH. I wish to mention that in the first half of 1992 the ABiH was not even yet a military structure. Whatever the decision of the Trial Chamber, maybe the Prosecution will certainly adhere to it but the Prosecution agrees with my learned colleague from the Defence side, there must be a guidance from the Trial Chamber to avoid such situations in future.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. It's twenty past 10.00. We'll have our traditional break, which will last half an hour. And we'll resume at twenty to 11.00 -- at ten to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Trial Chamber has considered this matter of documents and procedure with regard to the tendering of these documents. The Trial Chamber would like to remind everyone that when it comes to the pertinence, the Trial Chamber considers that a document tendered into evidence by one of the parties, be it the Prosecution or the Defence, to the extent that they are legal professionals tendering these documents, necessarily means that they will have checked the pertinence of the documents. It is up to the Defence and the Prosecution to speed up the process as much as possible and not waste any time by tendering documents which are of no consequence. So a priori, when one of the parties wishes to tender a document into evidence, that means that they consider it pertinent. As the pertinence, we may consider that a document may be pertinent because it has to do with the facts that the witness can shed more light on or because there is a direct or indirect link with the facts discussed here. So that means that by virtue of their very nature these documents are pertinent. Or else we may have another possibility, another situation, concerning documents which are not directly related to the facts discussed but deal with the period of time which is either close or more distant from the facts and causes of those facts but by the very nature of these documents, they may also prove to be pertinent. Now, the pertinence must be appreciated with regard to the political context, the economic context, the military context, and the historic one. Now the Trial Chamber believes that we have a fairly broad definition of this idea of pertinence. And once a party explains why they wish to tender a document and they explain the reasons, the reasons with regard to the context, the document in question at that stage becomes pertinent. A document that's tendered into evidence will take on probative value once the Judges decide so in the course of their deliberations. It is not simply because a document is tendered into evidence that by virtue of that very fact it becomes probative. Afterwards, in the course of our deliberations, we do appreciate the actual probative value of such a document. A document may prove to become probative because of a testimony but three months later perhaps another witness account may render it more relative, and it is up to the Trial Chamber to decide to what extent a document is probative or not. So if a party explains to us the reasons why they believe certain documents are pertinent, either because they're directly related to the facts or because they date from the same time period as the facts discussed or because it has to do with the political, economic, historical, and military context, at that stage you must explain to the Trial Chamber the usefulness of that document. So that having been said, if a document is produced and we are asked to accept it, and for it to be tendered into evidence we shall accept it; on the other hand, when the document is discussed, if somebody argues about the authenticity of the document, at that stage that document will be tendered for identification purposes and it will be up to the party having produced that document, if they wish for the said document to be finally tendered into evidence, to prove the authenticity of that document. We have had this situation earlier on with regard to this document. So for identification purposes, it is up to the party tendering it to prove that it is indeed genuine. It may well be that it is a false document and that it has escaped the vigilance of one of the parties in the course of their controls and checks. It may happen. And at that stage, of course the document will have to be withdrawn if the outcome of those checks is negative. The second point to be dealt with has to do with the documents which may be tendered in the course of the witness accounts on the part of expert witnesses. And in the course of such witness accounts, as we shall see shortly, at that stage documents will be produced in order to support the testimony and there will be quite a few documents there. If in the previous case, that is to say, a witness appearing before the Court, not an expert witness but an ordinary one, the documents are tendered in the course of the hearing, in the course of the cross-examination, as has been the case here, so no problem there. Now, concerning the expert witnesses, it would be desirable to the extent to which this is possible, since these expert witnesses already make a written statement - there is a structured statement and it leads us to think that they will be questioned according to that plan - and since there is a plan for this witness account which reflects the written statement, it would be desirable that the party introducing such a witness, it would be desirable for them to draw up a List of Documents relating to the questions they intend to ask and that with regard to every question they list the actual documents they intend to produce and tender it into evidence. Since the other party is familiar with the written statement, the Trial Chamber believes that there's no problem with providing the other party with the List of Documents. If in the course of the cross-examination the other party envisages to either argue against the documents or produce counter-documents, the other party at that stage would be able to, in order to save time, provide a separate List of Documents that they don't intend to argue against and also indicate, if they wish to do so, the documents that they are planning to counter by submitting other documents, if they wish to do that. For example, there is a document number 8 in the Prosecution list, and that number 8 is going to be counteracted, as it were, by another document. I mean, at that stage we would at least know that you would argue against this document on the basis of another document. And in practical terms, everybody will benefit. It will be sufficient for the Prosecution to follow closely the planned testimony on the basis of the written statement and refer in their list to the documents, and you would already have the list of the documents. You would be familiar with that list. And then, in order to save time, the Defence could mention, okay, documents 8, 15, 25, 28 are going to be argued against and we have a counter-document that we intend to submit. So it will benefit everyone. It would also be desirable if within the general framework of things, when the Prosecution examines the witness, also asks about the context, the overall context. It is not at all useless, and it also makes it possible for us to gain time. As to the Defence, it would also be desirable that when they produce documents which they say are pertinent, well, they see to it that such documents are not produced in order to refer to other cases. I am simply saying that we are dealing here with the case involving two people and not anyone else. So you should not start producing documents which would call into question the situation of anyone else, except in order to refer to a specific type of context. I don't think these documents should be analysed in order to look for indications about other people. Now, both the Prosecution and the Defence need to ask balanced questions, and we shouldn't get the impression that one party is focussing on one particular part of the context to the detriment of what the other party has done. Of course, if there is such imbalance, the Trial Chamber may intervene to ask questions about the overall context in order to establish this balance. Now, what we are all after is to speed up proceedings, to defend the rights of the accused, to defend the rights of the Prosecution, and as I've mentioned on more than one occasion, the rights of witnesses as well need to be protected. And we all wish to avoid repetition. And sometimes, due to repetition, we waste a considerable amount of time. In order to assure all sides, the probative value is something that the Trial Chamber decides about. It is not simply because a document is tendered into evidence that by virtue of that very fact it is considered as probative. The probative value is going to be determined by the Judges in the course of their deliberations. Now, more specifically, on the documents which were submitted, we have this document that was argued against. There will be an identification number for that document. It was the document signed by the Colonel General Ante Roso. In B/C/S, it says "General" and in English, it says "Colonel General." Now, I didn't know that there was a military rank of Colonel General. Either you're a colonel or else you're a general, but you can't be both at the same time. I really don't understand what the English translation means, but it does say "Colonel General." Now, that document in B/C/S and the English translation, we shall provide it with an identification number. Registrar, can you give us a number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, the B/C/S version gets the exhibit number DH35 ID; and the English translation gets the exhibit number DH35/E ID.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For identification purposes. All right, then. We also have a B/C/S document and the English translation of that document from the Croat Defence Council, dated the 10th of April, 1992. The document was drafted in the place called Grude, and it is signed by Mr. Mate Boban. This document was sent to all the headquarters at the municipal level of the Croat Defence Council. Now, we have it in B/C/S and in English. Registrar, can you give us a number, please. The final number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the exhibit number will be DH36 for the B/C/S version and DH36/E for the English translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] DH36 and 36/E. We have a document concerning a text of 24 articles, once again by Mr. Mate Boban. And it is about the organisation, the authority and administration on the territory of the Croat Community of Herceg-Bosna. This document is dated September 1992. It was published in 1992 and it was drafted in Mostar, the 3rd of July, 1992, English and B/C/S. Registrar, do please give us a number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, the exhibit number for the B/C/S version will be DH37, and the exhibit number for the English translation will be DH37/E.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you. We had a document in English and in B/C/S dated the 3rd of July, 1992 from Mr. Mate Boban. It concerns the appointment of Mr. Zec, who was appointed as president of the HVO in Travnik. It concerns the appointment of Mr. Krizanac, who was pointed as vice-president. Mr. Registrar, could we have an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the exhibit number will be DH38 for the B/C/S version and DH38/E for the English translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. If I have understood the matter correctly, there are another four documents. We'll try to speed up.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, thank you for your decision. We have another three documents, because you have just dealt with the fourth document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Don't forget to mention what relevance of each document is on each occasion. You must tell us why you consider that the document is pertinent in relation to a given context, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have another three documents. Mr. President, I would just like to say that, in accordance with your suggestion that we should indicate the source of the document, I indicate the source of the document on each occasion. I'm not going into whether these documents are in the favour or to the detriment of some of the accused in other cases, but all the documents that we have produced are relevant for the defence of General Hadzihasanovic, and this is the only purpose for which we tender them into evidence. In order to accelerate the proceedings, I suggest that I show the three remaining documents to the witness at the same time. The first document comes from the Official Gazette of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. And it's the decision of the constitutional court of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, which proclaimed all decisions about establishing the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna as illegitimate and all decisions concerning the establishment of the HVO and the establishment of executive power. It's a document of exceptional importance because the root of the conflict which is concerned in the indictment is contained in these decisions which are against the Constitution, which are non-constitutional. A second decision is a decision, and this is document was taken from the Kordic case. The second document that we are tendering is the attempt of the legally elected organs of power to have the HVO made part of the legal BH army forces. And this is an amended decree about the Armed Forces of Bosnia and Herzegovina. And in this document, they accept the HVO as part of the armed forces, providing that they recognise the command of the Supreme Command of the BH army. And the last document concerns the appointment of the witness Tomislav Rajic to the position of chief for the Municipality of Travnik. I think that this is a relevant document because it tells us something about the position of the witness during the period concerned in the indictment. I think we should show all three documents to the witness immediately so that he can say whether he recognises them and to enable the Trial Chamber to decide whether they should have them marked for identification or whether they should immediately accept them into evidence. Thank you. Your Honour, I apologise. The last document, that mentions the appointment of Mr. Rajic, was found in the archives of the HVO in Zagreb. The Defence found it in the course of its investigations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Witness, you have three documents, and the Defence would like to hear your comments on the three documents. The simplest way to proceed would be for you to tell us about the document from Mr. Bruno Stojic, the document that concerns your duties. This document came -- comes from Mostar on the 29th of March, 1993. I have it in B/C/S and in English. I was reading it in B/C/S. Mr. Rajic, as far as the third document is concerned, do you recognise the document in which your appointment is mentioned? What can you tell us about this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I recognise it.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Rajic, is this the document which appointed you to the duties mentioned in the document?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV RAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I suggest that this document be accepted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Registrar, can we have an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the B/C/S version will get the exhibit number DH39, and the English translation gets the exhibit number DH39/E.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Let's move on to another document. It's a decision from the constitutional court, dated the 18th of September, 1992. We have the English translation and we have the text in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Rajic, are you aware of the fact that the constitutional court of Bosnia and Herzegovina adopted a decision according to which all laws of Herceg-Bosna were declared to be against the Constitution, as well as the decision on its establishment?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV RAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not familiar with that, but the document that I had is now at the registrar. I didn't have a good look at it, so I'm not in a position to comment on it now. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Could you just tell me which decision you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: It's on the other side. It's a decision of the 18th of November, 1991, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV RAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Look, I haven't had the opportunity of reading this yet. I haven't seen it before. I never received this document before. This is the Official Gazette of RBiH. It's dated the 18th of September, 1992. At the time, my office didn't receive that Official Gazette, but I do know - and I haven't had the time to read everything yet - but I see the judges from the constitutional court have participated in the work, but it's customary to mention the judges who participated and to mention whether there are any separate opinions or not. In my opinion, this decision, I as a lawyer and on the basis of the experience I've had in Bosnia and Herzegovina, I can't -- this is an Official Gazette, but taking certain decisions in this manner is something that is questionable. Whether this constitutional court was composed in a manner that we are not aware of, I don't know, but they used the building of the constitutional court in Sarajevo and then perhaps they adopted such a decision. I would have to see who the judges were in the constitutional court who took this decision and then I would be able to comment on the authenticity of such a decision. But as I have said, this is the first time I've seen it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Trial Chamber would like to point out to the witness that this decision was signed by the president of the constitutional court, Mr. Ismet Dautbasic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Dautbasic, a professor at the School of Law and the president of the constitutional court.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That was my professor at the law faculty. I don't know whether he was the president of the constitutional court, but I'm saying that it is customary to mention in the introduction to the decision who the members of the constitutional court were who were involved in adopting a certain decision. At least, that's my experience to date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So the witness has said that this decision, in his opinion, is questionable, given that the composition of the Chamber is not mentioned in the document. This is what the witness has told us. Since this decision appeared in the Official Gazette of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, we need a number for this document. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, the B/C/S version will get the exhibit number DH40, and the English translation will get the exhibit number DH40/E.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. And the last document that we have, Defence counsel has explained the relevance of the documents and told us that it is a document signed by Mr. Izetbegovic, the president of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. It's a document that concerns the Armed Forces of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and the text concerns integrating the HVO within the national army. Witness, as far as this last document is concerned -- he doesn't have it? On the basis of my knowledge of B/C/S, I can see that the document is -- comes from a military publication. I'm turning to the Defence. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's the Official Gazette that has published all the documents that concern the army and the Presidency adopted it in the course of 1992. And they were previously established in the Official Gazette, in the official journal of Bosnia and Herzegovina -- previously published in the official journal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Defence counsel has shown you a document. What do you have to say about the contents of the document, if you are familiar with the document? What can you tell us about it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All I can say is that this is the first time I have seen it. I didn't receive the Official Gazettes of the BH army. The Official Gazettes of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, I didn't receive them either at the time. And nor am I aware of my colleagues, Muslims, Bosniaks, receiving them because of the blockade of Sarajevo. It's possible that they did receive these gazettes, but I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
