utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, in accordance with your decision, you can accept this document into evidence as it was published in the Official Gazette, it could be -- or it could be marked for identification so that the Defence could subsequently tender this document into evidence through other witnesses, if they know anything about this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, the Prosecution. Before you take the floor, I'd like to point out that this document was signed by Mr. Izetbegovic on the 6th of August, 1992 in Sarajevo, and it was published in the Official Gazette of the RBiH army republic, and this is a decree law. What does the Prosecution have to say about this text of a military nature?

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, as my learned colleague herself suggested - and this is the understanding of the Prosecution that it is in compliance with the Chamber's decision - this document should only be marked for identification. Defence may or may not tender it later on via a different -- another witness. This witness has said he has never seen this document and he cannot comment on it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So this document will be marked for identification. Mr. Registrar, could we have a number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the exhibit number will be DH41, marked for identification for the B/C/S version; and the English version will get the exhibit number DH41/E, marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you. The Defence may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, for the sake of the transcript, I would like to point out that the decision of the constitutional court is important also because the Prosecution refers to it in the third amended indictment, in the addendum under item 6, where it also accepts the fact that the constitutional court proclaimed that these laws were illegal.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And as the witness has said that this is the first time he has seen the document, I would like to ask the witness whether Mr. Harmon showed him the same document when he was being examined in the Blaskic case.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV RAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that document. Not at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'll move on to another subject. I don't have any other documents to show you, and I will soon be concluding my cross-examination. Would it be correct to say that at the beginning of 1993 the sporadic conflicts in 1992 between the BH army also extended to the Busovaca and Gornji Vakuf municipalities? Are you aware of this fact?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV RAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday we spoke briefly about roads. Is it true to say that Central and Northern Bosnia and the Croatian border were linked up by roads that went through Gornji Vakuf to Livno and Split; that is to say, through Prozor, towards Jablanica, and then through Western Herzegovina to the Republic of Croatia? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV RAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those were the routes that you could use to reach Croatia by going over the mountains.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Would it be correct to say that the area from Gornji Vakuf to Prozor and from Busovaca through Kiseljak and further on towards Western Herzegovina, those areas in 1993 were under the control of the HVO? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV RAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which areas in particular? It did control some areas. But as to which particular areas the HVO controlled and as to which areas the BH army controlled, I didn't participate in that and I couldn't say anything about that. But with regard to the events in Travnik, I'm familiar with this situation. I was there all the time, I performed certain duties there, so I know about this. And I know that when I would sometimes go to the sea, this is the route I would take.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I won't ask you any more questions about things you are not aware of. Is it correct that in the course of 1992 and the beginning of 1993 HVO and the army were jointly defending their front lines against the Serbs in the area of the municipality of Travnik?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV RAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those were not exactly joint defence lines. It was one line next to the other. And it is true that we had -- well, not jointly exactly, not together. A part of the front line was defended by the HVO and a part of it by the BH army, and we never interfered with one another or mixed or combined our operations.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is it correct, Mr. Rajic, that because of the outbreak of the armed conflict in the valley of Lasva and because of an ever more tense situation in the area, as early as March 1993 was the time when the HVO left the defence line in Vlasic against the Serb forces and started concentrating on securing and fortifying the defences of certain villages against the BH? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV RAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it is exactly the opposite. The first position against the Serbs, well, it was done by the HVO. They stopped the Serbs. Where those front lines were, well, the HVO stayed there up until the armed conflict between the BH army and HVO in Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that in Travnik itself the positions of the HVO or, rather, the positions held by the HVO Travnik Brigade are at the outskirts of town in the direction of Han Bila and Vitez? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV RAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Look, if you're asking an isolated question like that, yes. But it's also true that those communications were also controlled by the BH army perhaps 100 metres away, either closer to Travnik or further out, away from Travnik. I did say yesterday that as people were going into suburbs, well, it depended on the actual national structure of the suburb in question. And then there were the units of either the HVO army or the HVO there. And so -- then the said units would control that part.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could we go back to the situation on the 8th of May. You said that in the time of the armed conflict you were at Guca Gora on the 8th of May.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV RAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand. The 8th of May?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, the 8th of June, 1993. I do apologise. You were in Guca Gora on the 8th of June when the conflict broke out; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV RAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In the monastery itself, in the monastery -- or, rather, the church of Guca Gora, at the time when you arrived some civilian population was sheltering there, as well as some members of the HVO; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV RAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only partly, because there were no members of the HVO there. There were about ten members of the HVO together with me. We arrived there, and we found that everybody else was civilian. And we're talking about a part of the population, about one-third of the overall population of Guca Gora; whereas, the others early in the morning, before 8.00 in the morning, had already left in the direction of another village, together with the two priests, and most of the local members of the HVO. Only about ten or a dozen of us were left behind. And we would have gone away only we didn't know about what was going on, because you had to be crazy to stay. I mean, there were only a dozen of us and many more of them.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that ten or a dozen of you, whatever, following a suggestion from UNPROFOR, you took off your uniforms, you relinquished your arms, and you put on civilian clothes?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV RAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wasn't exactly a suggestion from UNPROFOR. We wanted to get rid of something that could have cost us our lives.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that when you finally set off together with the civilian population from the church or the monastery that you also took the valuables which had been left in the church, in the monastery?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV RAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is not true. We only took part of these things that could fit into a lorry, and the nuns told us to do so. Those of us who were able to load things, we did take some stuff. But you don't really have some -- a lot of time to think of what is valuable or not. Whatever we could get our hands on. And basically, to be quite honest, we didn't really care about taking the valuables. We just wanted to get out of there. Probably there were some valuables there, but I know for certain -- I do know it, that about 6 to 7 thousand books, the complete library was left behind in the monastery. For the sake of establishing the truth, perhaps you are not aware of it; the most valuable part there were the old books, written in the ancient Bosnian alphabet. And the priests, they probably felt it was dangerous. And before the outbreak of conflict in 1992, they moved it to the monastery in Imotski, as well as some valuable paintings that were sent to that monastery in Croatia, and some of the paintings a couple of years after, when we regained the monastery, they were sent back. And the rest --

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, this was what I wanted to ask you about. You answered the following question as well, so you're fully aware of the fact that the most valuable stuff from the monastery was taken in 1992 with full approval of the HVO government of Travnik in December 1992, and it was with the approval of the 3rd Travnik Brigade, and the decision was of the 10th of December, 1992, and they approved the transport of those valuables, and you have actually confirmed this. Now, I would just like to clarify one more thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President -- Mr. President, the last passage, was this a question or was it a comment by my learned friend? If it was a comment, I would like to have it removed from the transcript. Otherwise, my learned colleague can ask a question of the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] As I was saying, on page 53, line 5 through to 11, the Defence is implying that the witness has said things that he has not said. The Defence indicates that the 3rd Travnik Brigade intervened. So he's supposed to have said things that he did not say himself. So it would be better if you could put this question again, because your question was a leading one.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Rajic, even though you did reply previously, are you aware of the fact that, with the approval of the government of the HVO in Travnik in December - and there was an approval from the 3rd Travnik Brigade from the month of December - and following the proposals from the priests in the monastery of Guca Gora, the most valuable things were taken out of the monastery in December 1992 and they were taken to Imotski in the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV RAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not familiar with all those details that you've indicated, but I found out -- I heard that there had been things removed. Who approved it, how it happened, I don't know. But I personally participated in the return of those items. But as to when they were taken away, I don't know about the details. I know that the priests had taken things out. And as to what exactly was taken out, I found out only when it was all brought back in the summer of 1998, when I saw what had been preserved.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now we have a complete answer from the witness about what he knew. I do apologise if I inadvertently suggested something that you had not said before. I would like us to clarify one more thing, another answer you gave to one of the questions. When the Prosecution asked whether you knew who the Mujahedin were subordinated to, on page 42, lines 21 through to 25, you replied: "I do not know exactly to whom they were subordinated, but I do know that they were not subordinated to the brigade commander. On one occasion, when the joint committee was set up with the order to go to Orasac, and that committee was made up of Colonel Zimic, Solakovic - I don't know what his rank was -" and then the Prosecution interrupted you and said that you were confusing things. It is on page 43, line 1. The Prosecution interrupted you, and he said, "The witness is a bit confused." In order to clarify this confusion, I would like to ask a couple of questions of you. Is it correct that in January 1996, within this joint committee for the officers of the army and the HVO you were meant to go to Orasac? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Mr. President, I really have to -- to object at this point in time, because nowhere in the examination-in-chief did I address to this witness anything about the period of January 1996. And even though I think my friend is under the impression that cross-examination is as wide as she gets, I don't think the Trial Chamber should allow her to go on a witch hunt. This is January 1996.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, when deciding on the previous issues, you did say yesterday that we were allowed to ask questions separately about the events in 1996. I quoted specifically the page and the lines of the witness's reply to the question put to him by the Prosecution, "Do you know who the Mujahedin were subordinated to?" On page 42, lines 21 through to 25, the witness replied, and I have just quoted his reply from the transcript. But the Prosecutor -- the Prosecution interrupted on page 43, line 1, by claiming that the witness was a tiny bit confused, and now I would like to shed some more light on what the witness was going to say on that occasion. So I am not going beyond the general framework of the questions that had been asked and the reply that the witness tried to give, but he was interrupted.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: And I beg to differ, Mr. President, because I interrupted the witness to show him the period that I was referring to, and that's why I interrupted the witness. And I brought him back to the period that I was referring to, and he answered with respect to that period.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I continue, Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right, then. Continue, because as I've indicated yesterday, it would be interesting if the witness could tell us within the framework of this 1996 committee what were his conclusions or what are the events or the elements which make it possible for him to claim today that there were Mujahedin there. So it may be useful for the sake of the overall context.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In order to clarify this, I would like you to reply to the following question: Is it correct, even though you have referred to this earlier on, that in January 1996 you were a member of the joint committee of the officers of the BH army and HVO which was meant to visit Orasac as well? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV RAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was, so to say, an associate member of that committee, because it was a committee which was set up, it seems to me, from the top. I think Ivan Slavicek was appointed by the member of the Presidency of BH or the president of the federation, Mr. Zubak. And from the other side, I think that on behalf of the headquarters, General Rasim Delic appointed Mr. Zimic and not Simic, because Simic with an 'S' is generally a Serb surname, so let's not confuse things here. I forgot his first name and I don't know his rank, but he was also accompanied by Adnan Solakovic and they came from Sarajevo together with Slavicek. Now, as to whether it was in winter, I am not sure. I am not sure that it was in January 1996. The only thing I do know is that I myself was not in a position to visit Orasac with those people.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: May I just ask you another question so it might be easier for you to clarify, because I'm very interested in this as well. Before this committee left for Orasac, is it correct that Ivan Slavicek, who was a lieutenant -- or colonel, sorry, an HVO colonel and member of the joint committee, is it true that he went to Mehmet Alagic, who at the time was the commander of the 7th Corps, and asked him for permission in order for the committee to visit Orasac because he felt that Orasac, from a territorial point of view, was in the area of the 7th Corps? Is it correct?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV RAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is correct. It was not just Ivan Slavicek who went there but the other members went to Travnik to see General Alagic. I know that, because I was Slavicek's host in Travnik, and it was up to me to accompany them around, because I was familiar with the area.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: It is right, but this was happening about a fortnight to 20 days before this visit to Orasac.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV RAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I don't know if it was a fortnight. Maybe a couple of days less than that. But we needed that much time in order to organise, to arrange the visit. And Colonel Slavicek had to take off his military uniform and he had to wear civilian clothes when he went to visit Orasac.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that the committee members, Slavicek and others, were told by General Alagic that Orasac was not under the control of the 7th Corps but they had to go to the 3rd Corps? Is that true?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV RAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not quite. On the basis of talks, after these meetings - because I was hosting Slavicek - I found out and basically Slavicek told me that he was told that it was true that the area where Orasac was situated was indeed within the territorial area, within the area of competence of the already-set-up 7th Corps and it had been formed on the basis of the 3rd Corps of the BH army. And what I gathered from the conversation was that, and that in as far as the formations in fact are concerned it had to belonged to the 3rd Corps. And so we had to go and ask for permission from Zenica. The commander was called Mr. Mahmuljin.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is it true to say that you then went to Zenica and that the members of the committee went to the 3rd Corps command and afterwards Slavicek told you that he had received permission from Zubak Mahmuljin, who was at the time the 3rd Corps Commander?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV RAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, look, I can't exactly remember what you are saying now. It wasn't just one visit. It took seven to ten days to walk from Travnik to Zenica, from Zenica to Travnik, in order to go from one corps, from the 7th to the 3rd and back, and in order to get that permission. All I know is that Slavicek told me that Zubak had informed him, since the first request for a visit were not fruitful, that Slavicek wanted to return to Sarajevo. But he told me that Zubak said that it wasn't possible to return anywhere until the visit had been carried out. But as to which visit was concerned, whether the first or the second - I don't know how many visits there were exactly - after one of those visits, Slavicek was authorised to go to Orasac.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Rajic, at the time - before the visit to Orasac, that is to say - you found out for the first time that the Orasac camp was under the command of the 3rd Corps; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV RAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what I heard.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Any cross-examination for the other Defence team?

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. We have no questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before the Prosecution takes the floor for re-examination, Mr. Rajic, there is something I would like you to clarify. It concerns the activity of this defence secretariat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you tell us the exact date you left your position.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV RAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember the exact date, but it was in the summer of 1992. I didn't even leave that position in the sense of tendering my resignation or being relieved of my duties. And I repeated this yesterday. I simply continued working, to the extent that this was possible, given the situation. I continued to work for the needs of the HVO and the Muslims in my secretariat worked on strengthening the units in our area, the Muslim people's units. That was at the beginning of the summer of 1992. We remained in a building, so to speak. The documents you have about people who were part of the reserve forces and civilian defence, who were part of recruits or who have to do with the centre for monitoring and surveillance, unfortunately I have to say that the divisions were based on ethnic affiliation. But very soon there were open conflicts in neighbouring municipalities - for example, in Novi Travnik in July or August, and in September 1992 Novi Travnik had been definitively separated. Towards mid-January 1992, a conflict broke out in Busovaca. And I think that earlier on in Gornji Vakuf or, rather, in Skopje, I can't say exactly where - there were always conflicts - it was always difficult -- we were somewhere in the middle, and it was very difficult to preserve the peace. I said that in 1992, on the 20th of October, to be exact, the 20th of October, 1992, the commander of the Travnik HVO Staff was killed, the late Ivica Stojak. He was a member, not at that time but earlier on, when we tried to unify in Travnik. He was the deputy commander and he was involved in an attempt to establish a joint armed force in the territory of the municipality of Travnik, a force headed by a commander of Muslim nationality. I would also like to add something else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A minute ago you said when you were in the Guca Gora monastery you took off your HVO uniform. For how long had you been wearing that uniform?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV RAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I started wearing the uniform at the beginning of 1992. Travnik was attacked by the Serbian troops on the 19th of April, 1992. So it was during that period that I started wearing my uniform. Perhaps -- perhaps it was then, but it was certainly not more than a month before that date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that yesterday you said that you had the rank of commander. What was your rank when you were in uniform, up until June 1993?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV RAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't have a rank of any kind. I was a secretary. There was a state of war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you didn't have a military rank of any kind. You were an ordinary secretary.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV RAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. I had a JNA rank that I had obtained after having served in the JNA. I had the rank of a reserve lieutenant. But that rank didn't mean anything in the subsequent formations of the military in Bosnia and Herzegovina, at least not for me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. And my very last question: Who paid you? Did you receive a salary?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV RAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time, I'm not even sure that we received a salary. What we did receive, I know that we received it from the municipality. That's where the funds -- but as to where the funds came from, I don't know. That's all I can say about the salary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Is there any re-examination for the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Mr. Rajic, my colleague in her cross-examination showed you numerous documents, some of which were admitted into evidence and some of which were marked for identification. Tell the Trial Chamber, in your opinion and from your understanding of the military and all that has been -- transpired, if in your opinion that these documents that you recognise and that were admitted into evidence, in your opinion, gave any authority to any military organisation in Bosnia during the period of the 1st of January to March 1994 to condone or ignore looting, shooting, and murder in the municipality of Travnik, by any of the units of the said existing military bodies at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the witness is being asked to express his opinion about the contents of documents, and he has said that he doesn't know most of them. And in particular, he is asked about his opinion on the application of international law. This is the responsibility of the Trial Chamber. The Trial Chamber decides on legal matters. I don't think that this is the kind of question that can be put to the witness, and I don't think that the witness can express any opinions of this nature.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. You have understood that the Prosecution would like you to answer this question and that the Defence has argued that you're not a specialist in humanitarian law, and in addition it's not for you to express your opinion on the way certain documents were used. And nevertheless, the Trial Chamber notes that you have been shown certain documents, so you have read them. You were familiar with some of them and you weren't familiar with others. We have taken note of this fact. But to clarify a certain matter for the Trial Chamber, as a lawyer and given your current position, when you discovered these documents, which aren't contested, since some of them appeared in the Official Gazette and you said that you found out about them at the end of 1992 - you can't say when exactly, though - but as a lawyer, when you discovered these documents and after you had read them, what was your opinion? I'm asking your legal opinion of these documents. As a lawyer, how did you view these documents which appeared or which came through official organs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've told you about the documents that I saw and about the documents I received. As far as the documents that I did not receive, I have already testified about this today, and for me certain documents are very much questionable. For example -- their relevance is questionable. For example, a decision of the constitutional court. Well, my question is: Did the president of the constitutional court use his position to take the decision that he did take? I know that in practice when such decisions are taken, it says, "The constitutional court, composed of," and then you mention the judges who compose it. In the decision I saw today, I didn't see the composition of the chamber. On the other hand, the document in which -- there is something else I'd like to say about the constitutional court. I saw that they referred to the Constitution of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and they spoke about the Constitution of Bosnia and Herzegovina. But as to whether they left out that "Republic" on purpose or whether that is the real name, I don't know. As far as the document which was forwarded to the staffs, you said it said "Colonel General," and it said "Ante Roso, General" and the seal wasn't circular. On the copy that I had, the seal wasn't totally circular. I saw that the coat of arms was different in the middle of that seal. It was different from the coat of arms that the HVO or, rather, the Croatian Community used, later the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna. As far as the HVO documents are concerned which were received, the ones that I saw, I didn't have the opportunity of seeing some of them because it was a time of war. And when you receive documents, you don't have the time. I wasn't following all the events, I wasn't chronicling all the events, I was an active participant, and until the very last day I was trying to avoid a conflict in Travnik, if this was at all possible. But the HVO documents which arrived, in my opinion they were temporary decisions. These were attempts to find one's bearings, function somehow in a given area, in an area where the central authorities weren't functioning, in an area where the state that we had elected as an independent state was disintegrating. You didn't have any communication with the central organs of power. You would see the gradual development of nationalist tendencies in organs that were supposed to be joint organs. The HVO documents that I received -- I didn't receive the other documents at all in 1992 -- I don't remember, as the Secretary of National Defence - and you saw when I was appointed to the HVO - I don't think I received a single official document, neither the Official Gazette nor a decree nor anything else, from the documents that were shown today. So on the one hand, the situation is that you don't have any contact with the central organs of power that were legally elected and appointed after the elections. You weren't in a position to have contact with those organs. And what is worse, what was even worse at the time is that those organs were undermined. And this was my experience, and not just my experience but the experience of other Croats too. We experienced this as an abuse of those organs that were joint organs at one time and for the interest of only one ethnic group in Bosnia and Herzegovina. So these other documents from the HVO are, in my opinion, an attempt to survive in Bosnia and Herzegovina, an attempt on the part of the Croats to survive in that area. We didn't know what Bosnia and Herzegovina would look like, we didn't know what would happen. Given the passage of time, this may appear quite differently. But at the time when we were all alone, when we had been abandoned, when the International Community wasn't particularly interested -- and this is my opinion, because UNPROFOR were present in their white vehicles, they moved around, they had their checkpoints. But we thought that someone would come and solve the problems that existed. Unfortunately - and we are most to blame - everyone was allowed to start fighting everyone else. Blood started flowing, and then someone said, "That's enough now. Let's start again." I'd like to say that in Travnik there was the inception of something that is now being implemented in Travnik, given the pressure exerted by the International Community. And that was the only place in Bosnia and Herzegovina up until the war and after the war in which the people themselves tried to form some sort of a joint army which didn't have any connections with the JNA or the Territorial Defence or the HVO or the Croats or the Muslims. However, this attempt failed. A group of people who had been elected and appointed in Travnik were involved in this attempt. This was at the beginning of 1991, I think. I think it was in February. And at the head of the group - and I was a member of that group, and I'm proud of this fact - Izet Tamburic, a Muslim, was at the head of that group. However -- I don't know how to explain this to you, but for people living in democratic countries, you know that the person who is elected is in power; whereas, in our case those who were elected weren't in power. We had people who came from the shadows who were in power, from parties. We weren't elected in elections. I was appointed by the Municipal Assembly of Travnik. I wasn't on the list of a political party. It's not on that basis that I was appointed. I wasn't even a member of parliament, of the municipal parliament, so it wasn't possible for me to be elected from there. But given that I worked in the secretariat for two or three months -- two or three months before the elections and before the appointment, and given that I had certain knowledge of the military, which can be obtained in a school for reserve officers in the course of one year - it's not very extensive military knowledge - I had received military training to command and control units the strength of a company. I wasn't a military strategist capable of organising the defence of a town or capable of commanding large units, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Any other questions, Mrs. Benjamin? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Well, Mr. President, my question has not been answered as yet, and I do not know if it's going to be allowed or if it's denied. But if it is denied, then that is the end of the re-examination. If it's allowed, I'd really like to hear the witness's response.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Rephrase your question and do so slowly and try to make it concise. Witness, please pay careful attention to the question. And the Defence will also listen to the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Mr. Rajic, as a military experienced person, as a legal practitioner, and as a witness here in this case today, the Defence has produced and has shown you several documents in the course of the cross-examination. Some of the documents were tendered into evidence, and it is my question to you: Based on the documents that were tendered into evidence, with your knowledge, if it is in your opinion and your understanding that in any of those documents any authority was given to any military body, any military unit in the municipality of Travnik during the period 1993, and more specific, 1st of January, 1993 to March 1994 to either ignore or condone shooting, looting, and murder in the municipality of Travnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. The question goes beyond what one would expect as an answer. Is that why the Defence is standing up? We should limit the question to the following: On the basis of the documents that you had, in your opinion was a military unit given a certain military task? That's all we would like to ask. Can you answer this very simple question. On the basis of the documents that you had, was a unit established? And if so, which one? If you don't want to answer, don't answer the question. Either you can say that the documents -- well, it was the HVO that was constituted or the BH army, it was one or the other or both or neither of the two. A lawyer who sees such documents, what sort of conclusions can be drawn from the documents? Yes, the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, perhaps I understood this differently. This question was quite large in scope. I have understood the question to mean they want to ask whether documents allow a commander or military unit to kill, to maltreat, et cetera. Since we are talking about international law, which is applied regardless of what is contained in certain documents, I think that this concerns the application of international law and this is the responsibility of the Trial Chamber. The witness can't comment on this. And secondly, the witness isn't familiar with the documents from the BH army. He never saw them and he never read them. He can't say anything about them. And HVO documents, well, I think that he can't comment on them because yet again this is a witness who cannot express his opinions about this subject, and this is why we stand by the objection that we raised.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The Trial Chamber will withdraw for a few minutes to see whether we will authorise this question or not. Please don't move. --- Break taken at 12.23 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. After having deliberated about the question asked by the Prosecution, it's the opinion of the Trial Chamber that this is a matter for the Trial Chamber to decide on, so it's not for the witness to answer such a question, since the witness doesn't possess all the elements and all the documents. He's only seen certain fragmentary documents, some from the HVO, and he hasn't even seen all of them. So in such a case it's not possible to ask the witness such a question. Are there any other questions you have for the witness, Mrs. Benjamin? I thought that this was the last one.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: I'm grateful, Mr. President. And I'm happy to inform you that this concludes the re-examination of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mrs. Benjamin. Witness, thank you for having come to The Hague to testify here. Your testimony took almost two days, but it was important for you to be present in order to inform the Judges of the events that you witnessed as a result of the position you held. Thank you for having answered the questions to the extent that this was possible for you. You provided us with very long and detailed answers. We followed your answers with great interest. And this concludes your testimony here. We wish you a good trip home, and we wish you all the best in your professional life. We wish you much success when exercising your profession as a lawyer. I'll now ask the usher to escort you out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We have a second witness, who is on standby, but I think it's time to have a break now. So if you agree, we'll have a break now to allow the interpreters to have a break, because the questions and answers require a lot of concentration and the pause will be much appreciated. We'll resume at five to 1.00, and you may take the floor then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Withopf, you have the floor, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, can we please go into private session?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Registrar, this is going to be a private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Witness ZB, you will now have to answer the questions that will be put to you by representatives of the Prosecution. The Prosecution is to your right. One of the two representatives of the Prosecution will be asking you some questions. Their examination will start in a few minutes' time, and we will continue tomorrow, since at 1.45 we will have to adjourn. When the Prosecution has concluded its examination, Defence counsel for the accused, who are to your left - there are six of them, but only two of them will be asking you questions - they will proceed with their cross-examination, which will be based on the Prosecution's examination-in-chief. If necessary, the three Judges who are before you may also ask you questions at any time if they think it might be useful to clarify certain matters contained in your answers. If things are not completely clear, we might feel it necessary to ask you some questions. Take your time to answer the questions put to you. If the question is complicated, ask the person putting it to you to rephrase it clearly. If there are any problems, inform the Judges of the problem. I have to inform you that when you testify, after having made a solemn declaration, you have to tell the truth. If you don't tell the truth, if your testimony is false, you could be punished. This could involve either a fine or a prison sentence up to seven years in prison, or both penalties could be imposed on you. This shows the importance of your testimony. In addition, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence of this Tribunal provide in one of its Rules that when you're asked to respond to a question, if the answer might incriminate you, in such a case this can't be used against you. So these are the provisions covering the testimony of witnesses before this Tribunal. We have another 15 minutes. We can make good use of these 15 minutes. And without wasting any more time, I'll let the Prosecution take the floor now.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President, Your Honours. Mr. President, can we please go in private session again, since the first series of questions or the answers to the first series of questions may identify the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. We'll go into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Now that we're in open session, the Trial Chamber will resume the proceedings tomorrow at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 18th day of February, 2004, at 9.00 a.m. 24
